Autocorrelation-robust significance test for the Lagrange \(\chi^2_{np}\) trend

Source: R/lr_trend_test.R
lr_trend_test.Rd

Assesses whether the decreasing "bias" trend that Lagrange regularization acts on (the slope \(\beta_1\) of \(\chi^2_{np}(T_1)\) against the window start \(T_1\)) is statistically distinguishable from what the estimation noise produces on its own. Three tests are reported: a naive OLS \(p\)-value (invalid here, because adjacent rolling windows overlap and \(\chi^2_{np}(T_1)\) is heavily autocorrelated); a heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent (Newey–West) \(p\)-value; and a parametric AR(1)–GARCH(1,1) bootstrap, which is the appropriate test.

Usage

lr_trend_test(rolling, log_price, B = 199, cores = 1L, hac = TRUE, seed = NULL)

Arguments

rolling

An "lppls_rolling" object from lppls_rolling(); it must carry the fit_args slot (rebuild with a current version of the package if absent).

log_price

Numeric vector of log-prices the rolling was built on; its length must equal rolling$n_full.

B

Integer, number of bootstrap replicates (default 199).

cores

Integer, number of cores for parallel::mclapply() (default 1; ignored on Windows).

hac

Logical, whether to also compute the Newey–West HAC \(p\)-value (default TRUE).

seed

Integer or NULL; a base seed that makes the bootstrap paths reproducible. The caller's random number stream is left as it was. When NULL, the paths are drawn from the caller's stream.

Value

An object of class "lr_trend_test": a list with the observed slope beta1 and lambda (\(= -\beta_1\)); the naive p_ols / se_ols; the HAC p_hac / se_hac; the bootstrap p_boot, standardized distance z and null vector null; the fitted noise model (ar1, garch = c(omega, alpha1, beta1), and persist \(= \alpha + \beta\)) with its valid flag; the effective replicate count B, the window count n_windows, and the call.

Details

The bootstrap fits an AR(1)–GARCH(1,1) model (via stats::arima() and the tsgarch package) to the residuals of the full-window (\(T_1 = 1\)) LPPLS fit, simulates fresh noise paths, adds them to the fitted LPPLS curve, and repeats the rolling calibration to build the null distribution of \(\beta_1\). The observed slope is compared against this null (two-sided). A validity guard is applied: if the fitted GARCH persistence \(\alpha + \beta \ge 1\) (IGARCH) the single-LPPLS null is misspecified, so the bootstrap is skipped, a warning is issued and p_boot is NA.

Requires the suggested packages tsgarch, xts and (for hac = TRUE) sandwich.

See also

lppls_lagrange(), lppls_rolling()

Examples

# \donttest{
if (requireNamespace("tsgarch", quietly = TRUE) &&
    requireNamespace("xts", quietly = TRUE) &&
    requireNamespace("sandwich", quietly = TRUE)) {
  set.seed(3630)
  N     <- 300
  log_p <- eval_lppls(seq_len(N), A = 8, B = -0.025, C1 = 0.0015, C2 = 0.001,
                      tc = N + 1, m = 0.6, omega = 8) + rnorm(N) * 0.01
  roll <- lppls_rolling(
    log_price = log_p,
    t1_seq    = seq(from = 1, by = 20, length.out = 8),
    hold_out  = 0, fh = 30,
    fit_args  = list(lower = c(0.1, 6, -0.03, 0.8),
                     upper = c(0.9, 13, -1e-14, 1e6),
                     m_init = 0.5, o_init = 8, num_searches = 1)
  )

  ## A single-regime series has no real trend, so the test should find none.
  ## Every bootstrap replicate repeats the rolling calibration; B = 9 keeps
  ## the example quick, but use 199 or more in practice.
  lr_trend_test(roll, log_price = log_p, B = 9, seed = 1)
}
#> Lagrange chi^2_np bias-trend test
#>   slope beta1 = -1.41e-08   (lambda = 1.41e-08)   over 8 windows
#>   OLS p       = 0.461      HAC (Newey-West) p = 0.453
#>   AR(1)-GARCH(1,1): ar1 = -0.02, alpha + beta = 0.838  [valid]
#>   parametric bootstrap: p = 0.556, z = 0.25  (B = 9)
# }
